mainTopic: חרוסת and לחם עוני, the מה נשתנה questions, and how the father tells the story of יציאת מצרים at the סדר.
overview: This amud opens by finishing the explanation of why מצה is called לחם עוני. A poor person eats a broken piece, and a poor couple bakes quickly. The גמרא then discusses חרוסת. If it is not a מצוה, it is brought to counter the harmful קפא in the bitter herbs. If it is a מצוה, as רבי אלעזר ברבי צדוק holds, it recalls either the apple tree (רבי לוי) or the mortar (רבי יוחנן), and אביי rules that it should be made both tart and thick. A new משנה then teaches that after the second cup the son asks מה נשתנה, and the father teaches the story at the son's level, beginning with disgrace and ending with praise. A ברייתא adds that someone must always ask, even a man alone or two scholars. רבא and רב ספרא reword the question about dipping, and רב and שמואל disagree about what the 'disgrace' is. The story of רב נחמן and דרו shows that the questions only exist to open the telling. The amud ends as a new משנה of רבן גמליאל begins; it continues on the next amud.

steps.title: So too here, a broken piece of מצה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its first explanation of לחם עוני: just as a poor person eats a broken piece, at the סדר we use a broken piece of מצה.
steps.simpleTranslation: So too here, we use a broken piece.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is wrapping up a comparison it started on the previous amud: a poor man usually eats only a piece of bread, so at the סדר the מצה is eaten as a broken piece.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word עוני in 'לחם עוני' is read as 'poverty.' Poor people rarely have a whole loaf, so the מצה over which we say the ברכה should be a פרוסה (broken piece). This line is the 'payoff' of that comparison.

keyTerms.meaning: A broken piece (of bread or מצה)
'Bread of poverty', the Torah's description of מצה
So too here (applies the comparison to our case)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for breaking the middle מצה (יחץ) and saying the ברכה on a broken piece at the סדר.

phrases.english: So too here, with a broken piece.
phrases.notes: This finishes the comparison: just as a poor person eats a piece of bread, so too here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Concludes the derivation from 'לחם עוני' that began on the previous amud.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The מצה of the סדר is used as a broken piece, like a poor person's bread.

steps.title: A second meaning of poor man's bread: baked in a hurry
steps.stepSummary: An alternative reading: a poor man heats the oven while his wife bakes right away, and מצה is likewise baked quickly.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another explanation: just as a poor man's way is that he heats the oven and his wife bakes, so too here, he heats and his wife bakes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different explanation of why מצה is called לחם עוני. It has nothing to do with a broken piece. It is about how the bread is baked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A poor couple has little firewood, so they work together and bake fast before the fire dies. מצה is also baked quickly, with no waiting, so the dough does not become חמץ. Here 'poverty' describes the rushed process, not the size of the piece.

phrases.english: Another explanation:
Just as the way of a poor person is
he heats the oven and his wife bakes,
phrases.notes: They work at the same time so the scarce fuel is not wasted.

phrases.english: so too here as well,
he heats the oven and his wife bakes.
phrases.notes: The מצה is baked right away so it cannot rise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second reading of לחם עוני alongside the broken-piece reading.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: מצה is 'poor man's bread' because it is baked quickly, the way a poor couple bakes.

steps.title: If חרוסת is not a מצוה, why bring it?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה saying חרוסת is not a מצוה, then asks why it is brought to the table at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Even though חרוסת is not a מצוה.' And if it is not a מצוה, why is it brought?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line of the משנה about חרוסת and asks a clarifying question: what is it for, if it is not a מצוה?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא of the משנה says חרוסת is brought to the table but is not a מצוה. That seems strange, since the סדר is carefully arranged around מצוות. So the גמרא wants to know the practical reason for bringing it.

keyTerms.meaning: A paste of fruit, nuts and spices eaten with the מרור

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין חֲרוֹסֶת מִצְוָה.
phrases.english: Even though חרוסת is not a mitzva.
phrases.notes: This is quoting the משנה, the view of the תנא קמא.

phrases.english: And if it is not a מצוה,
for what reason do they bring it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי לָא מִצְוָה, מִשּׁוּם מַאי מַיְיתֵי לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the משנה, חרוסת, unrelated to the לחם עוני discussion.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The practical purpose of חרוסת according to the view that it is not a מצוה.

steps.title: חרוסת protects against a harmful substance in the bitter herbs
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי answers that חרוסת is brought because of קפא, a harmful substance in the מרור that the חרוסת neutralizes.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אמי said: Because of the poison (קפא).
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אמי answers the question: חרוסת is there for health reasons, to counteract something harmful in the bitter herbs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Bitter vegetables like חסא (lettuce) were thought to contain a harmful substance. Dipping the מרור in חרוסת neutralizes it. So according to the תנא קמא, חרוסת is a medical precaution, not a ritual.

keyTerms.meaning: A harmful or poisonous substance found in vegetables

phrases.english: רבי אמי said:
Because of the poison (in the bitter herbs).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: חרוסת is brought to neutralize the harmful substance in the מרור.

steps.title: A chain of remedies for vegetable poisons
steps.stepSummary: רב אסי lists which food cures the harmful substance in each vegetable, ending with hot water as a cure for all of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אסי said: For the poison of lettuce, radish. For the poison of radish, leeks. [For the poison of leeks, hot water.] For the poison of all of them, hot water.
steps.whatsHappening: Building on the mention of קפא, רב אסי adds related medical advice: a chain of remedies for vegetable 'poisons'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a side discussion triggered by the word קפא. Each harmful vegetable has a counter-food. Hot water works as a general remedy for all of them. The bracketed line about leeks is a textual addition found in some versions.

phrases.english: רב אסי said:
For the poison of lettuce, radish.
For the poison of radish, leeks.
[For the poison of leeks, hot water.]
phrases.notes: The words in brackets appear only in some versions.

phrases.english: For the poison of all of them, hot water.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אַסִּי: קָפָא דְחַסָּא — חָמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands on the idea of קפא raised by רבי אמי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each vegetable's harmful substance has a remedy, and hot water cures them all.

steps.title: An incantation to say while waiting for the remedy
steps.stepSummary: While the remedy is being brought, the person should recite a folk formula addressing the poison.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the meantime, let him say this: 'Poison, poison, I remember you, and your seven daughters, and your eight daughters-in-law.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the medical side discussion with a short incantation to say while waiting for the cure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is folk practice recorded by the גמרא. It does not change any halacha about חרוסת. It simply completes רב אסי's medical advice.

phrases.english: In the meantime, let him say this:
'Poison, poison, I remember you,
and your seven daughters, and your eight daughters-in-law.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the medical digression begun by רב אסי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: While waiting for the remedy, one recites a formula addressing the poison.

steps.title: What מצוה does חרוסת fulfill?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי אלעזר ברבי צדוק, who says חרוסת is a מצוה, and asks what that מצוה is.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'רבי אלעזר ברבי צדוק says it is a מצוה,' etc. What is the מצוה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the other opinion in the משנה and asks what makes חרוסת a מצוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the תנא קמא, רבי אלעזר ברבי צדוק holds that חרוסת has religious meaning. The גמרא wants to know what it is meant to remind us of.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the מצוה (what is its purpose)?

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי צָדוֹק אוֹמֵר מִצְוָה וְכוּ׳.
phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok says it is a מצוה, etc.
What is the מצוה?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the תנא קמא's view to the opposing view in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the מצוה of חרוסת commemorates.

steps.title: Remembering the apple tree or the mortar
steps.stepSummary: רבי לוי says חרוסת recalls the apple tree. רבי יוחנן says it recalls the mortar of the slavery in מצרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי לוי says: in memory of the apple. רבי יוחנן says: in memory of the mortar.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים answer the question, each giving a different thing that חרוסת commemorates.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי לוי connects it to the apple trees under which Jewish women in מצרים gave birth (תחת התפוח עוררתיך), a symbol of redemption. רבי יוחנן connects it to the טיט, the clay and mortar of the hard labor. One view recalls hope, and the other recalls suffering.

keyTerms.meaning: Mortar or clay used for bricks

phrases.english: Rabbi Levi says:
In remembrance of the apple.
phrases.notes: Based on שיר השירים: 'Under the apple tree I awakened you.'

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan says:
In remembrance of the mortar.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 7 with two opinions.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Either a remembrance of the apple tree (רבי לוי) or of the mortar (רבי יוחנן).

steps.title: Make חרוסת both tart and thick
steps.stepSummary: אביי concludes that חרוסת should be made tart for the apple and thick for the mortar, satisfying both views.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Therefore it must be made tart and it must be made thick. Tart, in memory of the apple. Thick, in memory of the mortar.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives the practical ruling: make the חרוסת so that it fits both opinions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of choosing between רבי לוי and רבי יוחנן, אביי combines them. Tartness, from apples, recalls the apple tree. A thick, clay-like texture recalls the mortar. The two views become two features of one recipe.

keyTerms.meaning: To make it tart or sharp

steps.whatToRemember: According to אביי, חרוסת is tart (apple) and thick (mortar), so both reasons are honored together.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
Therefore one must make it tart
and one must make it thick.
Make it tart, in remembrance of the apple,
and one must make it thick, in remembrance of the mortar.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the two opinions into one practical ruling.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: חרוסת must be both tart and thick.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says the spices recall the straw and the חרוסת recalls the mortar, which supports רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in accordance with רבי יוחנן: The spices are in memory of the straw. The חרוסת is in memory of the mortar.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that backs up רבי יוחנן's view that חרוסת commemorates the mortar.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא assigns meaning even to the ingredients. The stringy spices recall the straw (תבן) mixed into the bricks, and the paste recalls the mortar. This matches רבי יוחנן's slavery-based reason.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא in support of him

phrases.english: It was taught in accordance with Rabbi Yochanan:
The spices are in remembrance of the straw,
the charoses is in remembrance of the mortar.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies a תנאי source supporting one of the two views in step 8.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוחנן's view that חרוסת is זכר לטיט.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא stating that spices recall the straw and חרוסת recalls the mortar.

steps.title: Jerusalem spice-sellers called it a מצוה
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר ברבי צדוק reports that the shopkeepers in ירושלים advertised their spices as being 'for the מצוה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר ברבי צדוק said: This is what the spice merchants in ירושלים used to say: 'Come and take spices for the מצוה.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with a real-life report showing that people in ירושלים treated the spices for חרוסת as a מצוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This backs רבי אלעזר ברבי צדוק's own view in the משנה that חרוסת is a מצוה, not just a remedy. The sellers called the spices 'for the מצוה', which shows the common practice saw it as religiously meaningful.
steps.whatToRemember: The practice in ירושלים supports the view that חרוסת is a real מצוה, and its spices are part of the remembrance of slavery.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok said:

phrases.aramaic: כָּךְ הָיוּ אוֹמְרִים תַּגָּרֵי חָרָךְ שֶׁבִּירוּשָׁלַיִם:
phrases.english: This is what the small shopkeepers in Jerusalem used to say:
Come and take for yourselves spices for the מצוה.

steps.triggerLanguage: כָּךְ הָיוּ אוֹמְרִים תַּגָּרֵי חָרָךְ שֶׁבִּירוּשָׁלַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא and supports the view that חרוסת is a מצוה.
steps.raayaObject: The view of רבי אלעזר ברבי צדוק that חרוסת is a מצוה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The public practice of the Jerusalem spice-sellers, who called the spices 'for the מצוה'.

steps.title: The second cup is poured and the son asks
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says that once the second cup is poured, the son asks his father questions. If the son cannot ask, the father teaches him.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: They poured him the second cup, and at this point the son asks his father. If the son does not have the understanding to ask, his father teaches him.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It tells us when the questions of the סדר are asked: right after the second cup is poured.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Pouring the second cup before eating is meant to make the child curious, so he asks. The משנה does not give up when the son cannot ask. It puts the job on the father to teach him what to ask.

keyTerms.meaning: The second of the four cups

phrases.english: MISHNAH: They poured for him the second cup
phrases.notes: 'For him' means for the leader of the סדר.

phrases.english: and here the son asks his father.
phrases.notes: 'Here' means at this point in the סדר.

phrases.english: And if the son does not have understanding
his father teaches him.
phrases.notes: The father teaches him the questions.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ מָזְגוּ לוֹ כּוֹס שֵׁנִי וְכָאן הַבֵּן שׁוֹאֵל אָבִיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the discussion of חרוסת is finished.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After the second cup the son asks. If he cannot, the father teaches him.

steps.title: The four questions of מה נשתנה
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lists the four ways this night is different: only מצה, מרור, only roasted meat, and dipping twice.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why is this night different from all other nights? On all other nights we eat חמץ and מצה, but tonight only מצה. On all other nights we eat other vegetables, but tonight מרור. On all other nights we eat meat roasted, stewed, or cooked, but tonight only roasted. On all other nights we dip once, but tonight twice.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה now gives the actual questions the son asks. Each one compares a normal night to the סדר night.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every question follows the same pattern: 'other nights we do X, tonight we do Y.' The roasted meat question refers to the קרבן פסח from the time of the בית המקדש. Dipping twice means the vegetable dipped early in the סדר plus the מרור dipped in חרוסת.

keyTerms.meaning: What is different / Why is it different

steps.confusionAlert: This list is not exactly the מה נשתנה in our הגדה. Here there is a question about roasted meat, which applied when the קרבן פסח was eaten, and there is no question about reclining. Also, the line 'on all nights we dip once' is challenged later in the גמרא: רבא and רב ספרא reread it (steps 17–20), and רב ספרא's version, 'we do not dip even once', is the one in our הגדה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source of the מה נשתנה that every Jewish child says at the סדר.

phrases.aramaic: מָה נִשְׁתַּנָּה הַלַּיְלָה הַזֶּה מִכׇּל הַלֵּילוֹת.
phrases.english: Why is this night different from all other nights?

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁבְּכָל הַלֵּילוֹת אָנוּ אוֹכְלִין חָמֵץ וּמַצָּה,
phrases.english: For on all other nights we eat leavened bread and matza,
this night, it is all matza.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁבְּכָל הַלֵּילוֹת אָנוּ אוֹכְלִין שְׁאָר יְרָקוֹת,
phrases.english: For on all other nights we eat other vegetables,
this night, bitter herbs.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁבְּכָל הַלֵּילוֹת אָנוּ אוֹכְלִין בָּשָׂר צָלִי שָׁלוּק וּמְבוּשָּׁל,
phrases.english: For on all other nights we eat meat roasted, stewed, or cooked,
this night, it is all roasted.
phrases.notes: The קרבן פסח must be roasted.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁבְּכָל הַלֵּילוֹת אָנוּ מַטְבִּילִין פַּעַם אֶחָת,
phrases.english: For on all other nights we dip once,
this night, twice.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה נִשְׁתַּנָּה הַלַּיְלָה הַזֶּה מִכׇּל הַלֵּילוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the content of the questions the son asks, as mentioned in step 12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The questions are about מצה, מרור, roasted meat, and dipping twice.

steps.title: How the father teaches the story
steps.stepSummary: The father teaches according to the son's level. He begins with shame, ends with praise, and explains the פרשה of ארמי אובד אבי to its end.
steps.simpleTranslation: The father teaches him according to the son's understanding. He begins with disgrace and ends with praise. He explains the verses starting from 'An Aramean tried to destroy my father' until he finishes the whole section.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה now moves from the questions to the answer. It tells the father how to tell the story of יציאת מצרים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Three rules are given: match the child's level, go from shame to glory, and use the פרשה of ביכורים (ארמי אובד אבי) as the text to explain. The story must be told as a journey from a low point to a high point.

keyTerms.meaning: 'An Aramean tried to destroy my father' (דברים כו:ה)

steps.whatToRemember: The father teaches at the son's level, starts with shame, ends with praise, and explains ארמי אובד אבי.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the structure of מגיד in our הגדה. The גמרא will soon discuss what 'disgrace' means.

phrases.english: And according to the understanding of the son
his father teaches him.
phrases.notes: Here he teaches the story itself, not the questions.

phrases.english: He begins with disgrace and ends with praise.
And he expounds from 'An Aramean tried to destroy my father,'
phrases.notes: From the declaration said when bringing ביכורים.

phrases.english: until he finishes the entire section.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְפִי דַּעְתּוֹ שֶׁל בֵּן אָבִיו מְלַמְּדוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the son's questions to the father's answer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Teach at the child's level, from disgrace to praise, explaining ארמי אובד אבי fully.

steps.title: Who asks the questions if there is no wise son
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says the wise son asks. If not, the wife asks. If not, the man asks himself. Even two תלמידי חכמים ask each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: If his son is wise, the son asks him. If he is not wise, his wife asks him. If not, he asks himself. Even two Torah scholars who know the laws of פסח ask each other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins and quotes a ברייתא that adds to the משנה. It explains what to do when there is no son able to ask.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה spoke only about a son. The ברייתא shows the questions must be asked no matter what, even by the man himself. Even scholars who already know the answers must ask, because asking is part of the מצוה, not just a way to get information.
steps.whatToRemember: The questions are always asked: by a son, a wife, oneself, or even two scholars to each other.
steps.confusionAlert: The scholars already know the answers. They still ask because asking is part of the night's obligation.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is why a person alone at the סדר still says מה נשתנה.

phrases.english: GEMARA: The Rabbis taught:
If his son is wise, he asks him.
And if he is not wise, his wife asks him,
and if not, he asks himself,
phrases.notes: If there is no wife, or she cannot ask.

phrases.english: and even two Torah scholars
who know the laws of Passover
ask each other.

steps.triggerLanguage: גְּמָ׳ תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: חָכָם בְּנוֹ שׁוֹאֲלוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands the משנה's rule that the son asks by covering cases where there is no capable son.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The questions must be asked by someone: son, wife, oneself, or fellow scholars.

steps.title: The משנה's question about dipping
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the line of the משנה about dipping once on other nights and twice tonight.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why is this night different from all other nights? On all other nights we dip once; on this night we dip twice.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes one line from the משנה's list of differences so it can examine the wording. This is a setup for the challenges that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: As written, the line suggests that dipping once is the normal routine on every night. The next steps will question whether that is accurate.

keyTerms.meaning: What is different / why is it different
We dip (food into a liquid or relish)

phrases.aramaic: מָה נִשְׁתַּנָּה הַלַּיְלָה הַזֶּה מִכׇּל הַלֵּילוֹת,
phrases.english: Why is this night different from all the nights,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁבְּכָל הַלֵּילוֹת אָנוּ מַטְבִּילִין פַּעַם אֶחָת,
phrases.english: for on all the nights we dip one time,
this night — two times.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה נִשְׁתַּנָּה הַלַּיְלָה הַזֶּה מִכׇּל הַלֵּילוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the list of four differences from step 13 to study one line closely.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: On ordinary nights we dip once; on Pesach night we dip twice.

steps.title: רבא objects that we do not have to dip every night
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenges the משנה's wording, since there is no rule that we must dip once every day.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא objected: Is it true that on every day we cannot get by without dipping once?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks the wording of the משנה. It sounds as if dipping once is required every night, and that is not true.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'we dip once' makes single dipping sound like a fixed rule. In reality, nobody is required to dip at all on a normal night. So the comparison in the משנה seems inaccurate.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say...? (introduces a challenge)
It is not possible to manage without

phrases.english: Rava strongly objected to it:
Is that to say that every day it is impossible
without dipping one time?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording quoted in step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's phrase 'on all nights we dip once'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The phrase implies a daily requirement to dip, but no such requirement exists.

steps.title: רבא rewords it in terms of obligation
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that the משנה means: on other nights we are not obligated to dip even once, but tonight we dip twice.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said, this is what it teaches: On all other nights we are not obligated to dip even once; this night, twice.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers his own challenge by rereading the משנה. The difference is about obligation: normally there is none, and tonight there is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The contrast changes from 'once vs. twice' to 'no obligation at all vs. two dippings.' This removes the false impression of a daily rule. It does, however, suggest that tonight's two dippings are an obligation.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it is teaching

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said, this is what it teaches:
for on all the nights we are not obligated
to dip even one time,
this night — two times.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves רבא's challenge from step 17 by rereading the text.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to describe single dipping as a nightly routine.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה contrasts no obligation on other nights with two dippings tonight.

steps.title: רב ספרא objects: an obligation for children?
steps.stepSummary: רב ספרא challenges רבא's rewording: the extra dipping is only to get the children to ask, so it cannot be called an obligation.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ספרא objected: An obligation, for the sake of children?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב ספרא attacks רבא's answer. The double dipping is done only to make the children curious, so calling it a 'חיוב' is too strong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's version uses the word 'obligated' for tonight's two dippings. רב ספרא points out that a custom meant to prompt children's questions is not a real obligation. So רבא's wording does not fit either.
steps.confusionAlert: רב ספרא is not saying we skip dipping twice. He only objects to calling it an 'obligation,' because its purpose is to get the children to ask.

phrases.english: Rav Safra strongly objected to it:
An obligation for the sake of the children?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's answer from step 18.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Dipping twice is a way to stir the children's curiosity, not a true obligation.

steps.title: רב ספרא's wording: we do not dip even once
steps.stepSummary: רב ספרא rereads the משנה as: on other nights we do not dip even once, but tonight we dip twice. No obligation is mentioned.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב ספרא said, this is what it teaches: We do not dip even once; this night, twice.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ספרא gives the final version of the question. It simply describes what we usually do and what we do tonight.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This wording avoids both problems. It does not claim we must dip on other nights, and it does not call tonight's dipping an obligation. It just contrasts our normal habit with tonight's unusual behavior.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the version found in our הגדה: 'שבכל הלילות אין אנו מטבילין אפילו פעם אחת.'
steps.whatToRemember: Three readings: the plain משנה (once vs. twice), רבא (no obligation vs. twice), and רב ספרא (we don't dip at all vs. twice). רב ספרא's version is the one we say.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב סָפְרָא, הָכִי קָתָנֵי:
phrases.english: Rather, Rav Safra said, this is what it teaches:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין אָנוּ מַטְבִּילִין אֲפִילּוּ פַּעַם אֶחָת,
phrases.english: we do not dip even one time,
this night — two times.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב סָפְרָא, הָכִי קָתָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves רב ספרא's challenge from step 19 and closes the discussion of wording.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא's version made tonight's dipping sound like an obligation.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה describes behavior only: normally no dipping, tonight two dippings.

steps.title: What does 'beginning with disgrace' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's rule that the father begins with disgrace and ends with praise, and asks what the 'disgrace' is.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'He begins with disgrace and ends with praise.' What is meant by 'with disgrace'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line of the משנה from step 14 and asks a clarifying question. It is setting up the two answers that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה told the father to open his answer with something shameful, but did not say what. The גמרא wants to know which shameful part of our history is meant.

phrases.english: He begins with disgrace and ends with praise.
What is 'with disgrace'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic, returning to the line from step 14.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What content counts as the 'disgrace' the father should begin with.

steps.title: רב: our ancestors were idol worshippers
steps.stepSummary: רב says the disgrace is that our ancestors were originally idol worshippers.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: 'At first our ancestors were idol worshippers.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב gives the first answer. The shame is spiritual: our ancestors worshipped idols.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב, the low point of the story is the spiritual one, before אברהם. The praise is that we were brought close to serving 'ה.

phrases.english: Rav said:
'At first our forefathers were idol worshippers.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The disgrace is our ancestors' idol worship.

steps.title: שמואל: we were slaves
steps.stepSummary: שמואל says the disgrace is 'we were slaves' in מצרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And שמואל said: 'We were slaves.'
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל gives a different answer. The shame is physical: we were slaves to פרעה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For שמואל, the low point is slavery in מצרים, and the praise is our freedom. This ties the answer directly to the story of יציאת מצרים.
steps.whyThisMatters: Our הגדה includes both openings: 'עבדים היינו' (שמואל) and 'מתחלה עובדי עבודה זרה היו אבותינו' (רב).
steps.whatToRemember: רב: the disgrace is idol worship. שמואל: the disgrace is slavery.

phrases.english: And Shmuel said: 'We were slaves.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer to the same question that רב answered in step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The disgrace is that we were slaves.

steps.title: רב נחמן asks דרו about a freed slave
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן asks his servant דרו what a slave should say to a master who frees him and gives him silver and gold.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said to his servant דרו: A slave whose master sets him free and gives him silver and gold — what should he say to him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story from a סדר night. רב נחמן asks his servant a question that is really about the meaning of the night.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The freed slave with gifts is a picture of בני ישראל leaving מצרים with riches. רב נחמן is checking whether דרו understands what the night is for.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב נַחְמָן לְדָרוּ עַבְדֵּיהּ:
phrases.english: Rav Nachman said to Daru his servant:
A slave whose master takes him out to freedom,
and gives him silver and gold,
what should he say to him?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב נַחְמָן לְדָרוּ עַבְדֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a story that connects to שמואל's opening of 'עבדים היינו'.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What a freed and enriched slave should say to his master.

steps.title: דרו: he must thank and praise
steps.stepSummary: דרו answers that the slave must thank and praise his master.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: He must thank and praise.
steps.whatsHappening: דרו gives the obvious answer: a freed slave should thank and praise his master.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without meaning to, דרו has described the whole purpose of the סדר: thanking and praising 'ה for freeing us.

phrases.english: He said to him: He must thank and praise,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב נחמן's question from step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The slave must thank and praise his master.

steps.title: רב נחמן skips מה נשתנה and starts 'עבדים היינו'
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן tells דרו that his answer has exempted them from asking מה נשתנה, and he immediately begins 'עבדים היינו'.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: You have exempted us from saying 'מה נשתנה.' He began and said: 'We were slaves.'
steps.whatsHappening: Because דרו already raised the topic, there was no need to ask the questions. רב נחמן went straight to the answer, 'עבדים היינו.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The questions exist only to open the conversation about our freedom. Once that conversation has started, they have done their job. רב נחמן's opening with 'עבדים היינו' also matches שמואל's view.
steps.whatToRemember: מה נשתנה is a tool to start the telling of the story. If the topic is already open, we can go straight to 'עבדים היינו.'

phrases.english: He said to him: You have exempted us from saying 'Mah Nishtanah.'
He opened and said: 'We were slaves.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from דרו's answer in step 25.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The questions only serve to open the telling of the story. Once it has started, one begins 'עבדים היינו', as in שמואל's opening.

steps.title: A new משנה opens with רבן גמליאל's teaching
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה begins. רבן גמליאל starts to state a rule about anyone who did not say certain things.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: רבן גמליאל used to say: Anyone who did not say…
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא's discussion is over, and a new משנה begins with רבן גמליאל's teaching. This line is only the opening of his statement and sets up the full rule that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now, the גמרא was explaining the earlier משנה's rule of starting with disgrace and ending with praise. Now רבן גמליאל adds a new requirement: some things must actually be said aloud. The words 'כל שלא אמר' tell us that what is required here is speech, but we have not yet been told what must be said.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for 'our משנה.' It marks the start of a new משנה text.
'Used to say.' It introduces a teaching that this Sage regularly repeated.
'Anyone who did not say.' It opens a rule about what a person must say aloud.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not try to understand this line by itself, because the sentence is unfinished. It continues on the next amud: 'these three things on פסח has not fulfilled his obligation' (פסח, מצה, מרור).

phrases.english: MISHNA: Rabban Gamliel would say:
phrases.notes: 'מתני׳' marks the start of a new משנה.

phrases.english: Anyone who did not say
phrases.notes: The sentence is incomplete. What must be said comes on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the גמרא's discussion ended with רב נחמן and דרו in step 26, this opens a new משנה with a new teaching.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבן גמליאל begins a rule that a person who does not say certain things (named on the next amud) has not fulfilled his obligation. Only the opening words appear here.
